source_text: Apollinem facitis citharaedum atque divinum. Primum de Maia natus in insula Delo, Oblata mercede postmodum structor, obsecutus Laomedonti regi Trojanorum muros eduxit. Locavitque sese, quem deum seducti putatis: Ossibus cujus amor Cassandrae flagravit, Subdole quem lusit virgo, falliturque divinus. Officio vervecis potuit scire bicordem. Repudiatus enim discessit inde divinus. Terruit hunc virgo specie, quam ille deberet. Illa prior quae debuerat deum amavisse, Lasciviens qui Daphnem sic coepit amare: Et tamen insequitur, dum vult violare puellam; Gratis amat stultus, nec potuit consequi cursu. Vel, si deus erat, occurreret illi per auras. Sub tectis illa prior venit, remansit que divinus. Fallit vos gens hominum, nam victu tristi fuerunt. Admeti pecora quoque pavisse refertur. Lusibus impositis dum mitteret discum in altum, Sublapsum non potuit retinere: prostravit amicum: Ultimus ille dies fuit Hyacinthi sodalis. Si divinus erat, mortem praescisset amici.
pass_a_gloss: You make Apollo a cithara player and divine. First born from Maia on the island of Delos, afterwards with a wage offered he followed as builder to King Laomedon of the Trojans and he brought forth the walls. And he rented himself, whom you think is a god seduced: his bones were inflamed with love for Cassandra, the virgin cunningly played him and the divine one is deceived. By the office of a shepherd he was able to know the two-hearted one. For the divine one departed repudiated from there. The virgin terrified him with her appearance, which he ought to have. She who first ought to have loved the god, he who began to love Daphne lustfully: and yet he pursues, while he wants to violate the girl; the foolish one loves for free and he was not able to attain by pursuit. Or, if he was a god, he would have met her through the air. The girl came first under the roof and the divine one remained. The human race deceives you, for they were of sad food. It is also reported that he pastured the flocks of Admetus. With games imposed while he was sending the disc into the air, he was not able to retain the one who slipped: he laid low his friend: that was the last day of his friend Hyacinthus. If he was divine, he would have foreknown the death of his friend.

pass_b_english: You call Apollo a cithara player and divine. He was first born from Maia on the island of Delos; afterward, hired for a wage, he served King Laomedon of the Trojans as a builder and raised the walls. And he hired himself out, the very one you think is a god seduced: his bones burned with love for Cassandra; the virgin played him cunningly, and the divine one was deceived. By the work of a shepherd he came to know the two-hearted one. For the divine one was rejected and departed from there. The virgin terrified him with the very appearance he should have commanded. She who ought to have loved the god first, he who began to love Daphne in lust: and yet he pursues her, while he wants to violate the girl; the fool loves for nothing and could not overtake her by running. Or, if he was a god, he would have met her through the air. The girl reached shelter first, and the divine one remained behind. The human race deceives you, for they lived on wretched fare. It is also reported that he pastured the flocks of Admetus. During imposed games, while he hurled the discus into the air, he could not hold onto the one who slipped; he struck his friend down: that was the last day of his companion Hyacinthus. If he was divine, he would have foreknown his friend's death.

review.notes: The translation accurately reflects the Latin text. Pass A and Pass B are consistent with the source. The translation of 'Admeti pecora' as 'flocks of Admetus' is correct. The conditional 'Si divinus erat, mortem praescisset amici' is correctly rendered as 'If he was divine, he would have foreknown his friend's death'.
